title: Bhai Jaita becomes Jivan Singh
hook: the man who carried Guru Tegh Bahadur's head was embraced by the tenth Guru, who called his people the Guru's own sons

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Mani Singh wrote out the Granth at Damdama Sahib, letter by letter, as the Guru recited. Your line was the steady scribe. Did you do one thing exactly as asked? Today, we step back to an earlier, darker night. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

Delhi, in the square of Chandni Chowk. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, has just been executed on the emperor's order. His body lies where it fell, with guards around it, as a warning. Sikhs in the crowd are afraid even to be recognized. Then night comes, and with it, in the story, a storm and confusion. And one man moves toward the Guru's body when everyone else is moving away. He is a Sikh named Jaita. Today: Bhai Jaita becomes Jivan Singh.
screen: `CHANDNI CHOWK, AFTER THE EXECUTION.` → `GUARDS, AND A CROWD AFRAID.` → `ONE MAN MOVES TOWARD THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Bhai Jaita took the Guru's head, wrapped it, and carried it away from Delhi, traveling hard and in secret, all the way to Kiratpur and Anandpur, to the Guru's young son, Gobind Rai. Others in the story took care of the body, and a Sikh named Lakhi Shah burned his own house to cremate it unseen. But it was Jaita who arrived before the boy with his father's head. Here is the moment Sikhs remember. Jaita came from a community that the society around him counted low. The young Guru did not see that. Tradition says he embraced Jaita and said words Sikhs still repeat: Rangrete Guru ke bete. The Rangretas are the Guru's own sons. Not servants. Not followers allowed in at the edge. Sons. A whole people, looked down on by the society around them, named family in one sentence, because one of them had walked toward the Guru's body when others walked away. Years later, when the Khalsa was formed, tradition says Jaita took amrit and received a new name: Jivan Singh. Jivan means life. He became a commander and a poet in the Guru's service, and tradition says he fell at Chamkaur. So his story carries two names. Jaita, the man who carried a head through the night. Jivan Singh, the man the Khalsa made. Between them is the embrace: a boy whose father had just been killed, holding the man who brought him home, and making sure everyone heard what the Guru thought of him.
screen: `HE CARRIED THE HEAD TO ANANDPUR.` · `A COMMUNITY COUNTED LOW.` · `RANGRETE GURU KE BETE.` · `JAITA BECOMES JIVAN SINGH.` · then, large: `THE GURU'S OWN SONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone overlooked. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone the people around you tend to look past, or look down on. The worker nobody greets by name. The relative who always gets talked over. The kid who eats lunch alone. Notice how the young Guru answered Jaita: not with a private kind thought, but by calling him family where everyone could hear. What would it look like to treat this person as one of yours, openly? A greeting by name. A seat beside you. A word of credit in front of others. Let one answer come. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Jivan Singh. The name Bhai Jaita received in the Khalsa, after carrying Guru Tegh Bahadur's head to Anandpur and being embraced as the Guru's own son. Today's word.
Your line: the guru's own sons. Today, treat the person you thought of as one of yours, where others can see it: a greeting by name, a seat, a word of credit. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Jaita, later Bhai Jivan Singh, at Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi and at Anandpur, and the young Guru's words 'Rangrete Guru ke bete' are repeated as a sign that the Guru made the overlooked his own family.

notes: Editor pass: practice and carry reworked toward treating someone looked down on as family (day 822 already did a back-row, credit-giving practice); 'overlooked by everyone else' softened.
The phrase 'Rangrete Guru ke bete' and its Gurmukhi spelling ਰੰਘਰੇਟੇ ਗੁਰੂ ਕੇ ਬੇਟੇ: confirm; spoken as 'Rangrete' in the voice.
Jaita's community is described only as 'a community the society around him counted low' (Ranghreta / Mazhabi); confirm sensitive wording.
Route 'to Kiratpur and Anandpur' and Lakhi Shah (Lakhi Shah Vanjara) burning his house: tradition; confirm.
Jivan Singh as commander and poet, falling at Chamkaur: tradition; some accounts differ. Confirm.
'Jivan means life': simple Punjabi meaning, not a derived etymology; confirm it's acceptable under the claims rule.
Audit pass: 'done what no one else dared' (unsourced superlative, and Lakhi Shah also dared) changed to 'walked toward the Guru's body when others walked away'.
